section.title: Pentecost and the First Church
section.sectionRationale: This is the birthday of the church. The promised Spirit is poured out with wind and fire, the disciples declare the wonders of God in many languages, and the gathered nations hear. Peter interprets it all by Joel and the Psalms, proclaims the crucified and risen Jesus as Lord and Christ, and calls the crowd to repent. Three thousand believe, and the first church is formed, devoted to teaching, fellowship, bread, and prayer.
section.thesis: The exalted Christ pours out the promised Spirit, so that the gospel is proclaimed to every nation, the crucified Jesus is declared Lord and Christ, and a new Spirit-filled community is born that repents, believes, and shares its life together.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the coming of the Spirit with wind, fire, and tongues; the bewildered crowd from every nation; Peter's sermon from Joel and the Psalms proclaiming Jesus as Lord and Christ; the cut-to-the-heart response and three thousand baptized; and the shared life of the first church.

verses.text: When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place.
Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting.
They saw tongues like flames of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them.
And they were all filled with the Holy {{pneuma|Spirit}} and began to speak in other {{glossa|tongues}} as the Spirit enabled them.

units.label: The nations hear in their own languages
units.note: each one heard them in his own tongue

verses.text: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven.
And when this sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard them speaking his own language.
Astounded and amazed, they asked, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?
How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language?
Parthians, Medes, and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia,
Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome,
both Jews and converts to Judaism; Cretans and Arabs, we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!”
Astounded and perplexed, they asked one another, “What does this mean?”
But others mocked them and said, “They are drunk on new wine!”

units.label: Peter proclaims the risen and exalted Christ
units.note: God has made this Jesus both Lord and Christ

verses.text: Then Peter stood up with the Eleven, lifted up his voice, and addressed the crowd: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen carefully to my words.
These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It is only the third hour of the day!
No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel:
‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams.
Even on My menservants and maidservants I will pour out My Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.
I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and billows of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious Day of the Lord.
And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
Men of Israel, listen to this message: Jesus of Nazareth was a man certified by God to you by miracles, wonders, and signs, which God did among you through Him, as you yourselves know.
He was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross.
But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip.
David says about Him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me; because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.
Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope,
because You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.
You have made known to me the paths of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence.’
Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.
But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne.
Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay.
God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses.
Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.
For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand
until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’
Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and {{christos|Christ}}!”

units.label: Cut to the heart: three thousand believe

verses.text: When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?”
Peter replied, “{{metanoeo|Repent}} and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off, to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.”
With many other words he testified, and he urged them, “Be saved from this corrupt generation.”
Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.

units.label: The shared life of the first church
units.note: devoted to teaching, fellowship, bread, and prayer

verses.text: They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the {{koinonia|fellowship}}, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.
A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs.
All the believers were together and had everything in common.
Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need.
With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart,
praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The word plays on the sound of wind that fills the house as the Holy Spirit is poured out. The Spirit is the promised gift of the Father, given by the exalted Christ, who fills the believers and empowers their witness. Pentecost is the outpouring of the Spirit on the whole people of God.

glossa.gloss: Tongue, language. At Pentecost the disciples speak in other tongues, real human languages, so that the gathered nations each hear the wonders of God in their own speech. The sign reverses the scattering of Babel, gathering the nations to hear one gospel.

christos.gloss: Christ, Messiah, the Anointed One. Peter's sermon climaxes in the declaration that God has made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. He is the promised King from David's line, risen and enthroned, the one on whom the name of the Lord is called for salvation.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, to change one's mind and turn. Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do, and Peter calls them to repent and be baptized in Jesus' name. Repentance is the turning from sin to the crucified and risen Lord that opens the way to forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit.

koinonia.gloss: Fellowship, sharing, common life. The first believers devote themselves to the fellowship, holding things in common and sharing with the needy. It is a partnership created by the Spirit, expressed in teaching, table, prayer, and generous care for one another.

basic.context: This is the day the church is born. Fifty days after Passover, at the feast of Pentecost, the promised Holy Spirit is poured out on the waiting disciples with a sound like wind and tongues like fire. They begin to speak in other languages, and Jews from all over the world, gathered in Jerusalem, hear the wonders of God in their own tongues. Peter explains the event from the Old Testament, preaches Jesus crucified and risen, and calls the crowd to repent. Three thousand believe and are baptized, and Luke describes the shared life of this new community.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the chapter in its four beats: the Spirit comes, the crowd is amazed, Peter preaches, and the church is formed. The central questions are: what does the outpouring of the Spirit mean, how does Peter use the Old Testament to explain it, what is the heart of his gospel message, and what marks the life of a Spirit-filled church? Peter's sermon is the model: it interprets the moment by Scripture and drives to Christ and repentance.
basic.originalLanguages: The pneuma, the Spirit and wind, is poured out, and the disciples speak in other glossa, tongues, real languages heard by the nations. Peter's sermon climaxes in the declaration that God has made Jesus both Lord and christos, Christ. The crowd, cut to the heart, is told to metanoeo, repent, and the new community devotes itself to koinonia, fellowship, a shared common life.
basic.typology: Pentecost reverses Babel: where God once scattered the nations by confusing their languages, He now gathers them to hear one gospel, each in his own tongue. The feast of Pentecost celebrated the harvest and, in Jewish tradition, the giving of the law at Sinai; now the Spirit is given and a great harvest of three thousand is gathered. The fire that rested on the disciples recalls the fire of God's presence.
basic.christ: Peter's whole sermon is about Jesus: certified by God through miracles, delivered up by God's set plan yet crucified by lawless hands, raised from the dead as David foresaw, and exalted to God's right hand, from where He pours out the Spirit. The outpouring is proof that Jesus reigns. The climax is the declaration that God has made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ.
basic.god: The Father plans, foreknows, raises, and exalts; the Son is enthroned and pours out the Spirit; the Spirit fills and empowers the church. Salvation is God's work from beginning to end, and the promise of forgiveness and the Spirit is for all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself. God adds to the church daily those who are being saved.
basic.crossReferences: Joel 2 is the prophecy Peter says is being fulfilled. Genesis 11 records the scattering at Babel that Pentecost reverses. Psalm 16 and Psalm 110 supply Peter's proof that the Christ would rise and reign. Acts 2:42-47 becomes the pattern of church life echoed throughout Acts.
basic.oneStory: The exalted Christ pours out the Spirit He promised, and the gospel breaks out to every nation gathered in Jerusalem. The crucified and risen Jesus is proclaimed as Lord and Christ, thousands turn to Him, and a new Spirit-filled people is born. From this fire the mission will spread outward to the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
The chapter is held together by two frames. The first is a pair of matching verses: Peter quotes Joel's promise that 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' verse 21, and at the close of the sermon he says the promise belongs to 'all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself,' verse 39. Human calling and divine calling bracket the whole address. The second frame is a pair of lists, the nations in verses 9 to 11 and the practices of the new community in verses 42 to 47, so that the chapter moves from many peoples to one people.

Peter's speech is built like a careful argument. He answers the charge of drunkenness first, verses 14 and 15, then reads the moment through Joel, verses 16 to 21. He tells the story of Jesus in three beats, accredited, crucified and raised, verses 22 to 24. Two psalms follow as two proofs: Psalm 16 shows that the Messiah would rise, verses 25 to 32, and Psalm 110 shows that He would sit at God's right hand, verses 33 to 35. The conclusion, verse 36, opens with 'Therefore let all Israel know with certainty,' and lands on the one noun that matters, the crucified Jesus.

Luke also writes Pentecost as an answer to two earlier scenes. In Luke 3:21 and 22 the Spirit comes on Jesus while He is praying; here the Spirit comes on a praying company, Acts 1:14. Jesus' first public sermon in Luke 4:18 begins with the Spirit upon Him; Peter's first sermon begins with the Spirit upon the church. Luke also likes the word homothymadon, 'with one accord,' which turns up at Acts 1:14, 2:46, 4:24 and 5:12, and it marks the unity that holds the community together at each stage. The summary at verses 42 to 47 is the first of several such portraits, and Luke returns to the pattern at Acts 4:32 to 35 and 5:12 to 16.
context.historical:
Pentecost took its name from the Greek word for 'fiftieth.' It fell fifty days after the sheaf of firstfruits was waved, Leviticus 23:15 and 16, and its offering was two loaves baked with leaven, Leviticus 23:17. Along with Passover and Tabernacles it was one of the three feasts at which Israelites were to appear before the LORD, Deuteronomy 16:16, so Jerusalem was crowded. Many of the pilgrims were Jews of the Dispersion, from the Parthian and Median lands in the east to Rome in the west. The list in verses 9 to 11 is not tidy geography. It includes Judea, which has puzzled readers since it is hardly a foreign land, and it names Jews and converts to Judaism together, so the audience is at once ethnically Jewish and culturally many.

Most of these visitors would have known Aramaic or Greek, which makes the miracle more striking. The point of hearing 'the wonders of God' in each native tongue is not that nobody could otherwise have followed, but that the praise reached each person in the language of his own home and heart. The mockers who say 'They are drunk on new wine,' verse 13, are using a word for sweet, fresh wine, and Peter's reply that it is only the third hour, nine in the morning, appeals to ordinary custom.

Peter is speaking in the city where Jesus was executed some seven weeks earlier. The priestly leaders who handed Jesus over still hold power in the city and can arrest him, as chapter 4 will show, so his boldness is real. David's tomb, 'with us to this day,' verse 29, was a known monument in the city, and 1 Kings 2:10 records that David was buried in the City of David. Baptism was no strange rite. Jerusalem had many stepped immersion pools for ritual washing, and John's baptism of repentance was within living memory, so three thousand baptisms in a single day were logistically possible and religiously familiar.
context.canonical:
Pentecost gathers a long line of promise. Isaiah foretold that the Spirit would be poured out from on high until the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, Isaiah 32:15, and Ezekiel promised a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people so that they would keep His ordinances, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27. Joel, whom Peter quotes, widened the promise to sons and daughters, old and young, servants and masters. Behind all of these stands a wish of Moses. When the Spirit rested on Eldad and Medad in the camp and Joshua wanted them stopped, Moses answered, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!' Numbers 11:29. Pentecost is that wish granted.

Jesus had prepared the disciples for this day by teaching about the Counselor, John 14:16 and 17, by saying it was better for them that He go away so the Counselor could come, John 16:7, and by commanding them to wait in the city for the Father's promise, Luke 24:49 and Acts 1:4 and 5. John the Baptist had said the Coming One would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, Luke 3:16.

After chapter 2 the pattern repeats and widens. The Spirit falls on the Samaritans, Acts 8:14 to 17, on Cornelius' household, Acts 10:44 to 47, and on the disciples at Ephesus, Acts 19:1 to 7. When Peter explains Cornelius to the Jerusalem church he says the Spirit fell on the Gentiles 'just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning,' Acts 11:15, treating Pentecost as the pattern. The letters then explain what Luke narrates. Believers are baptized in one Spirit into one body, 1 Corinthians 12:13, the Spirit is the guarantee of the coming inheritance, Ephesians 1:13 and 14, and the promise made to Abraham reaches the nations so that all receive 'the promise of the Spirit through faith,' Galatians 3:14. The story ends where Revelation 7:9 sets it, with a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote for Theophilus so that he might know the certainty of the things he had been taught, Luke 1:3 and 4, and Acts 2 is the hinge on which that certainty turns. The Gospel ended with a promise, 'I am sending the promise of My Father upon you,' Luke 24:49, and Acts 1:8 said what the power was for. Here the promise lands. Luke wants his readers to see that the church is not a new religion improvised after a failed movement but the people Joel and Ezekiel were pointing toward, and that Jerusalem's own Scriptures explain what they have just seen.

He also wants readers to see how the message goes out. The tongues are praise, verse 11, and the explanation comes in plain speech, so the gospel is never left to be decoded by the amazed. Peter's address becomes a pattern for all later preaching in Acts: it takes a puzzling event, reads it by Scripture, centres on the crucified and risen Jesus, and presses for a decision. Finally, Luke closes with a portrait of the community so that readers who were not in Jerusalem can recognise the same life in their own assemblies. The three thousand are not the end of the story but the first sheaf of a harvest that Acts 1:8 says will reach the ends of the earth.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Luke gives us several kinds of material and each must be read for what it is. The wind, the flames, the many languages and the crowd are the circumstances of a founding event. The text says 'Suddenly' and 'filled the whole house'; it never tells later believers to wait for wind or to expect fire. The same is true of the daily shared meals and the selling of goods in verses 44 and 45. Acts 5:4 shows that ownership was not abolished, so these are free acts of love in a particular season, and the later churches that took collections for Jerusalem, as in Romans 15:26, show the principle carried on in other forms.

What does bind is what is spoken with a command or reinforced elsewhere. 'Repent and be baptized' is addressed to every hearer and extended to those far off, verses 38 and 39. The four things to which the believers 'devoted themselves,' verse 42, are things the letters expect of every church. The test that Luke himself models is this: when the narrative is echoed by the apostles' direct teaching, as the gift of the Spirit is in Galatians 3:14, it is normative; when it appears once as a feature of a unique day, it is description.

debates.question: Is Pentecost a once-for-all founding event, or a repeatable pattern for Spirit-baptism and tongues in every believer's life?

views.label: A unique, unrepeatable founding event
views.case: Pentecost fulfills a specific promise and inaugurates the church age; the tongues are known human languages that gather the nations, and Peter says the gift of the Spirit belongs to all who repent and are baptized, so every believer already receives the Spirit at conversion, Acts 2:38-39. The dramatic signs mark the founding moment.

views.label: A repeatable pattern of Spirit-empowering
views.case: Later outpourings in Acts, such as chapters 8, 10, and 19, and Peter's words that the promise is for all who are far off, suggest to some that a distinct empowering by the Spirit, sometimes with tongues, remains available and is to be sought by believers today.

debates.bearing: All agree the Spirit is given by the exalted Christ and that every Christian receives Him; the difference concerns whether a subsequent, distinct Spirit-baptism with tongues is a normative pattern. Either way the goal is the same: a Spirit-filled people who witness to Christ and call on His name to be saved.

debates.question: What does 'for the forgiveness of your sins' mean in relation to baptism in verse 38?

views.label: Baptism is the appointed moment at which forgiveness is received
views.case: The Greek preposition eis can mean 'for the purpose of,' and Peter joins baptism to the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit in one sentence. Ananias says to Saul, 'be baptized, and wash your sins away,' Acts 22:16. On this reading repentance, faith and baptism belong together as one act of turning to Christ, and forgiveness is promised in that act.

views.label: Baptism points back to forgiveness already granted
views.case: Eis can also mean 'with reference to' or 'because of,' as in Matthew 12:41, where the men of Nineveh 'repented at the preaching of Jonah.' Peter preaches elsewhere that 'everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name,' Acts 10:43, and Cornelius' household receives the Spirit before they are baptized, Acts 10:44 to 48. On this reading baptism is the outward sign and seal of a forgiveness received by faith.

views.label: One conversion with several parts, held together by Luke
views.case: Luke does not separate repentance, faith, baptism, the name of Jesus, forgiveness and the Spirit as if each could stand alone, and in the pattern of Acts they arrive in different orders. Peter's grammar notes the difference between the corporate command to repent, which is plural, and the individual call to be baptized, which is singular and applies to 'every one of you.' The point is that none may be left out, not that one is the mechanism of the rest.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that Peter calls for a whole turning to Christ that includes baptism in His name, and that forgiveness and the Spirit are given by Christ and not earned by the water. They differ on how tightly the sign and the gift are bound, which is why churches that love the same gospel baptize in different ways and on different grounds.

debates.question: Has Joel's prophecy been fulfilled, or only begun?

views.label: Fulfilled in the inauguration of the last days
views.case: Peter says 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel,' verse 16, and changes Joel's 'afterward' to 'in the last days,' reading the whole era from the Spirit's coming to the return of Christ as one stretch of time. The signs of verses 19 and 20 are then partly present in the darkness at the cross, Luke 23:44 and 45, and partly still to come before 'the great and glorious Day of the Lord.'

views.label: An application of Joel, with full fulfilment still ahead
views.case: Others note that the sun did not turn to darkness and the moon to blood at Pentecost, and take Peter to mean 'this is like what Joel described,' with the complete restoration of Israel and the cosmic signs awaiting the end. The Spirit on all flesh is a down payment, not the final fulfilment.

debates.bearing: Both agree that Peter treats Pentecost as the opening of what Joel promised and that the invitation of verse 21 is open now. They differ on how much of the prophecy has already arrived, and Peter's own words, which join the Spirit's gift to a coming day, leave room for both fulfilment and expectation.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke begins with a verb that English smooths over. The day of Pentecost 'came,' verse 1, but the Greek is a form of sympleroo, 'to fill up completely,' and Luke uses the same verb at Luke 9:51 of the days before Jesus is taken up. It is the language of a calendar being filled to the brim. The feast and the promise reach their fullness at the same moment.

The Spirit's work in the disciples is described with apophthengomai, 'to speak out,' in verse 4, and the same verb is used of Peter's address in verse 14 and of Paul's 'words of truth' in Acts 26:25. It is the verb for solemn, weighty utterance, the root of the Greek word for a pointed saying, and Luke uses it in both places to show that the sound in the house and the sermon in the street are both Spirit-given speech. In verse 4 the speech is in heteraiis glossais, 'other tongues,' while verses 6 and 8 call the same thing 'language,' dialektos, in the sense of one's own native speech. The content is 'the wonders of God,' ta megaleia tou theou, verse 11: praise and recital of what God has done. This is worship in many languages. The proclamation that calls for repentance comes after, in Peter's common speech.

The word for 'pour out' in verses 17, 18 and 33 is ekcheo. Joel's Hebrew verb is shaphak, used also in Zechariah 12:10 of the 'spirit of grace and supplication' poured on Jerusalem, and the Greek Old Testament translates it with ekcheo. Peter's verse 33 says the exalted Jesus 'has poured out what you now see and hear,' so the verb that Joel gave to God now belongs to Jesus. In Acts 10:45 the same verb is used again when 'the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out' on the Gentiles. In that phrase and in Acts 2:38 the 'gift of the Holy Spirit' means the gift that is the Spirit Himself, as Peter's 'You will receive' in verse 38 shows.

In verse 23 God's 'set plan' is horismene boule. The verb horizo means to mark with a boundary and gives English 'horizon,' and boule is God's deliberate counsel. The pair appears again in Acts 4:28 of the 'hand and will' that decided beforehand what Herod and Pilate would do. Next to this, 'foreknowledge,' prognosis, makes the cross neither an accident nor a trap.

When the crowd is 'cut to the heart,' verse 37, Luke uses katanyssomai, a verb of piercing built on the root of nysso, the word John uses of the soldier's spear in John 19:34. The listeners feel the word as a thrust. Peter's reply joins a plural imperative, 'repent,' with a singular third person imperative, 'let each one of you be baptized,' so every hearer must act for himself. His closing appeal, 'Be saved from this corrupt generation,' verse 40, takes its adjective, skolios, 'crooked,' from the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5, which condemns a crooked and twisted generation. He tells them to step out of Israel's wilderness story and into the new one.

The tenses in verse 47 repay attention. 'The Lord added' translates an imperfect verb, so He kept on adding day after day, and 'those who were being saved' is a present participle: an ongoing stream of people in the process of being rescued, the same form Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 1:18.

typology.fulfillment: At Babel the LORD confused the language of the earth so that the people 'will not understand one another's speech' and scattered them, Genesis 11:7-9. At Pentecost a crowd gathered from the scattered nations hears one message, each in his own language. The correspondence is the reversal of a judgment into a gathering. The escalation is that Pentecost does not erase the languages: the nations stay who they are and are made one in Christ, until the multitude of Revelation 7:9 stands before the throne from every tongue. The type is also incomplete, because Luke does not call Pentecost the undoing of Babel, so the link is a fitting reading, not a stated one.

At Sinai God came down in fire with thunder, and later Jewish tradition tied the feast of Pentecost to the giving of the law. Luke does not say so, but the images fit: wind, a sound from heaven and fire on each person. Another contrast is visible in the numbers. After the golden calf 'about three thousand of the people fell dead,' Exodus 32:28; at Pentecost about three thousand are added to the believers, verse 41. The escalation is from a law written on stone to the Spirit who writes it on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33 and 2 Corinthians 3:3. Because Luke is silent, the Sinai link should be held as an illustration.

Pentecost was the harvest feast of the first grain, brought to the LORD as firstfruits. The coming of the Spirit and the first great ingathering of believers fits that picture, and the New Testament uses the same language: Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20, believers have 'the firstfruits of the Spirit,' Romans 8:23, and James calls believers a kind of firstfruits of God's creatures, James 1:18. The correspondence has limits. The two loaves were baked with leaven, a reminder that this harvest is gathered from an imperfect people, not that Christ's church is sinless.

typology.type: Moses' wish and the Spirit on the seventy, Numbers 11:25-29
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit rested on seventy elders and then on Eldad and Medad, and Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets. At Pentecost the wish becomes a fact: the Spirit rests on men and women of every rank, verses 17 and 18. The correspondence is the sharing of the Spirit beyond a chosen few. The escalation is that the Spirit is given no longer to leaders for a task but to a whole people as a permanent gift, verse 39. The type falls short because the Spirit on the seventy was passing and tied to Moses, whereas the Spirit now is given by the enthroned Christ and stays.

typology.type: David the prophet-king and his tomb, Psalm 16 and 2 Samuel 7:12
typology.fulfillment: Peter points out that David 'died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day,' verse 29. David is a true type of the King who would come: he was anointed, he suffered, and he was promised an heir on his throne. Yet the type breaks at the grave, because David's body saw decay, Acts 13:36, while the One whom God raised did not, Acts 13:37. The escalation is from a king who died and awaited the resurrection to a King who rose and reigns. The correspondence also reveals Christ's authority, since David himself calls his descendant 'Lord,' verse 34.

study.christ:
Peter's sermon climbs in steps, and each step is chosen. Jesus is first named as 'Jesus of Nazareth,' a man, verse 22, accredited by miracles that the crowd had seen. He is then crucified, but 'by God's set plan,' verse 23, so that the cross is placed inside the purpose of God rather than outside it. He is raised, because 'it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' verse 24. The line is not only that God raised Him but that death could not keep Him. He is exalted to the right hand, verse 33, and from that throne He gives the Spirit. The sermon ends with a title for the One the crowd crucified: 'both Lord and Christ,' verse 36.

Psalm 16 is Peter's proof of the resurrection. David wrote of 'Your Holy One' not seeing decay, but David's own tomb was occupied. Peter reasons that David 'was a prophet,' verse 30, who knew God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne, 2 Samuel 7:12 and 13, and who therefore 'spoke about the resurrection of the Christ,' verse 31. Paul argues the same way at Acts 13:35 to 37. Psalm 110 makes the second proof. David did not ascend into heaven, yet 'The Lord said to my Lord' speaks of someone at God's right hand. Jesus had put that very question to His opponents, Mark 12:35 to 37, and Peter now answers it.

The most striking link is the last. Joel had said that the LORD Himself would pour out His Spirit and that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD would be saved. Peter says Jesus has poured out the Spirit, verse 33, and then says Jesus is 'Lord,' verse 36, so that the name on which everyone must call, verse 21, is the name of Jesus. The Baptist had foretold this, Luke 3:16, and Jesus had promised, 'I am sending the promise of My Father upon you,' Luke 24:49. Christ receives the Spirit from the Father, verse 33, and gives Him to His people, so that He is the head who is anointed first and shares the anointing. 'Christ' itself means 'anointed one,' and the Anointed now anoints.

The chapter also leads to Christ by contrast and by pattern. Where the Spirit descended on Jesus alone at the Jordan, Luke 3:22, He now descends on many; where Jesus' words in the synagogue, Luke 4:18, began with the Spirit on Him, His church begins with the Spirit on them. Romans 1:4 says He was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' and Peter's 'made Lord and Christ' belongs with this, as the public enthronement of One who was always the Son.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The wind and the flames are signs of God's presence, not coded portraits of Jesus. The tongues are not a symbol of the Son. What leads to Christ here is the apostolic preaching itself, which Luke has recorded in order that his readers might follow Peter's own path from the Scriptures to the risen Lord.
study.god:
Pentecost shows the three persons of God at work without confusion and without division. The Father promised, Acts 1:4, and 'the promised Holy Spirit' is received from Him, verse 33. The Son, exalted at the Father's right hand, pours out the Spirit. The Spirit fills the disciples and enables the speech. The result is that one act of salvation is accomplished by the Father's plan, the Son's reign and the Spirit's power. Peter's closing words, 'all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself,' verse 39, say that the God who called Abraham is the God who is calling now.

The chapter holds sovereignty and responsibility in one sentence. Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and the same verse says 'you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death,' verse 23. Luke does not soften either half. God is not the author of their lawlessness, and the plan does not excuse them, which is why they are cut to the heart and told to repent. The doctrine of God that emerges is a God whose purposes run through even a murder without being stained by it, as the church prays in Acts 4:27 and 28.

God here is generous without distinction. The Spirit falls on sons and daughters, young and old, menservants and maidservants, verses 17 and 18, which crosses the lines of sex, age and class that most societies draw. The promise reaches 'you and your children and all who are far off,' verse 39, echoing the covenant promise to Abraham and his offspring, Genesis 17:7, and Isaiah's 'Peace, peace to those far and near,' Isaiah 57:19. At the same time, the calling is particular: 'whom the Lord our God will call.' Luke places verse 21, where everyone who calls is saved, beside verse 39, where God calls, and does not explain how both are true. The chapter invites trust in both, as Paul later does in Romans 10:13.

The God of this chapter is a God of presence. At Sinai the fire fell on a mountain, and in Exodus 40:34 the glory filled a tent. Now the flame comes to rest on each person, so that the people are the dwelling, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 3:16. God also keeps building: 'the Lord added to their number daily,' verse 47. It is His church, and the growth is His work.

He is also a God of joy. The believers eat 'with gladness and sincerity of heart,' verse 46, and David's psalm in verse 26 says, 'my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices.' Judgment is not absent, since Joel's day of the Lord is darkened in verses 19 and 20, but it stands beside a way to be saved.

For worship, the first thing the Spirit prompts is not an argument but praise: 'the wonders of God' are declared before any sermon is preached. The right response to this God is to praise Him together, to call on His name, and to take up the daily life of teaching, bread and prayer.

crossReferences.note: The promise that Pentecost keeps. Jesus told the disciples to wait for the gift the Father promised, said they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit in a few days, and named its purpose: power to be His witnesses to the ends of the earth. Acts 2 is the arrival and Acts 1:8 is the outline of everything that follows.

Peter's text, quoted at length. Joel speaks of the Spirit poured out on all people, wonders in heaven and earth, and deliverance for everyone who calls on the name of the LORD. Peter changes 'afterward' to 'in the last days' and presents Joel's wide promise as open to every hearer now.

The scattering at Babel, where the LORD confused the language of the whole world. Pentecost gathers people from the scattered nations to hear the wonders of God in their own languages. Luke does not name the connection, but the vocabulary of language and nations invites the comparison.

Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. The Spirit had rested on seventy elders and then on two men in the camp, and Moses rejoiced. At Pentecost the wish is granted at a scale Moses could not have imagined, with the Spirit given to women and men of every station.

The psalm Peter uses to prove the resurrection. David's confidence that God would not abandon his soul to the grave or let His Holy One see decay cannot be said of a man whose tomb is still in Jerusalem, so Peter reads it as David's prophecy of the Messiah rising. Paul uses it the same way in Acts 13:35 to 37.

One of the most quoted Old Testament verses in the New Testament. 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at My right hand' shows David addressing his own descendant as Lord. Peter reads it as the enthronement of the risen Jesus, from where He pours out the Spirit, and Hebrews 1:13 and 10:12 build on the same verse.

The new covenant promise of cleansing water, a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people. Peter's call to repent, be baptized and receive the gift of the Spirit lines up with these three promises, which is why the new birth and the gift of the Spirit belong together in the early church.

After the golden calf, about three thousand people fell dead at Sinai. At Pentecost about three thousand are added to the believers. The numbers are the same and the direction is the opposite. Luke does not draw the contrast, but readers steeped in the Torah would have felt the weight of it.

John the Baptist's prophecy that the One coming after him would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Acts 1:5 recalls it, and Pentecost shows both parts: the Spirit who fills and the fire that rests on each head. Jesus is the baptizer, so the Spirit's coming is His act.

At Cornelius' house the Spirit falls on Gentile hearers, and Peter asks who can refuse them baptism, since 'They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!' The scene confirms that the promise 'to all who are far off' in Acts 2:39 includes the nations, and it shows that the Spirit may come before baptism.

Luke's second summary of the church's shared life repeats the first, with one heart and soul, shared goods and no needy among them. The repetition marks the shared life as a recurring outflow of the resurrection and the Spirit, not a single burst of enthusiasm, and the fuller description there shows how the distribution worked.

Paul quotes Joel 2:32, 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' and says there is no distinction between Jew and Greek because the same Lord is Lord of all. He reads the Lord of Joel as Jesus, just as Peter does in verses 21 and 36.

Paul explains what Pentecost made possible: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body,' Jews and Greeks, slaves and free. The disciples' separate flames resolve into one body in which every believer shares the same Spirit, so Pentecost is the origin of the church's unity.

The scattered nations of Babel and the gathered nations of Pentecost come to their end in a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' standing before the throne. The Spirit's first work in many tongues is the first fruit of this final scene.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with the Spirit of God hovering over the waters, Genesis 1:2, and with God breathing life into the man He formed, Genesis 2:7. After the fall the Spirit is mostly given to a few, for a task and for a time. The prophets then promise a day when this will change, and Pentecost is that day: the breath that made the first man is now given to a new people.

The chapter answers two earlier failures. At Babel humanity tried to make a name for itself and was scattered into languages it could not share, Genesis 11:4 to 9. Here those scattered nations hear the wonders of God and are gathered into one body. At Sinai a nation was made in fire and the law was given, but the people broke the covenant within weeks. The new covenant of Ezekiel 36 and Jeremiah 31 promises what the law could not do: a heart changed from within. Pentecost is where that new covenant begins to take effect, with forgiveness and the Spirit offered to all who turn.

It also sets up everything after it. Acts 1:8 outlined the mission in three rings, Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth, and each ring now has a seed in the crowd. The Pentecost pilgrims returned to Cappadocia, Egypt, Rome and Arabia carrying what they had heard. Luke will later show the Spirit crossing each boundary in turn, to the Samaritans in Acts 8, to Cornelius in Acts 10 and to the disciples in Ephesus in Acts 19. Paul's letters take the same Spirit as the believer's seal and down payment, Ephesians 1:13 and 14, a firstfruits of the harvest still to come, Romans 8:23.

The end of the story answers the beginning of this chapter. The Bible closes with the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come,' Revelation 22:17, and with every nation, tribe, people and language gathered in worship, Revelation 7:9. What began in a room in Jerusalem, with one message in many tongues, becomes the song of the whole new creation. The believers of Acts 2 who devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer are the first picture of a people who will one day live in the presence of God without end, with the Spirit as the pledge that the day is coming.

quiz.q: What happened when the Holy Spirit was poured out at Pentecost?

options.text: The disciples were filled with the Spirit and spoke in other tongues, so the gathered nations heard the wonders of God.
options.note: This is exactly what Luke records: the Spirit fills them and they declare God's wonders in many languages.

options.text: A sound like wind and tongues like fire appeared over the disciples.
options.note: True signs of the moment, but the heart of the event is the Spirit filling them so the nations heard the gospel in their own tongues.

options.text: The apostles performed healings to prove they were not drunk.
options.note: The signs of wind, fire, and tongues, not healings, marked Pentecost; Peter answered the charge of drunkenness with Scripture.

options.text: The temple was filled with the glory of God and the priests fell down.
options.note: This does not describe Pentecost; the Spirit fell on the disciples in the house where they were gathered.

quiz.q: How did Peter explain what the crowd was seeing and hearing?

options.text: As the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy that God would pour out His Spirit in the last days.
options.note: Peter says plainly, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.

options.text: As a fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy.
options.note: Correct in general, but Peter names the specific prophecy of Joel about the outpouring of the Spirit.

options.text: As a special blessing given only to the apostles for their office.
options.note: Peter says the promise is for the crowd and their children and all who are far off, not the apostles alone.

options.text: As a sign that the law was being given anew from Sinai.
options.note: Peter points to Joel and the Spirit's outpouring, not to a new giving of the law.

quiz.q: What is the climax of Peter's sermon about Jesus?

options.text: God has made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ.
options.note: This is the summit of the sermon in verse 36, the risen Jesus enthroned as Lord and Messiah.

options.text: God raised Jesus from the dead because death could not hold Him.
options.note: A true and central claim, but the sermon climaxes further, in the declaration that Jesus is Lord and Christ.

options.text: Jesus was a great teacher approved by God through miracles.
options.note: Peter does say God certified Jesus by miracles, but that is his starting point, not the climax that Jesus is Lord and Christ.

options.text: Jesus will return soon to restore the kingdom to Israel.
options.note: That is not the point of this sermon; Peter proclaims the crucified and risen Jesus as Lord and Christ.

quiz.q: When the crowd was cut to the heart and asked what to do, what did Peter tell them?

options.text: Repent and be baptized in Jesus' name for forgiveness, and receive the gift of the Spirit.
options.note: Peter's answer in verse 38 joins repentance, baptism, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit.

options.text: Repent and turn from their sins.
options.note: Repentance is essential and part of the answer, but Peter also called them to baptism and promised forgiveness and the Spirit.

options.text: Keep the law more carefully so they might be forgiven.
options.note: Peter did not point them to law-keeping but to repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Jesus.

options.text: Wait quietly to see whether God would forgive them.
options.note: Peter did not counsel passive waiting; he called for repentance and baptism with the promise of forgiveness now.

quiz.q: What marked the shared life of the first church?

options.text: Devotion to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, with glad and generous sharing.
options.note: Luke's summary in verses 42 to 47 lists exactly these marks of the new community.

options.text: Meeting together and sharing their possessions with those in need.
options.note: True and part of the picture, but it leaves out their devotion to teaching, breaking of bread, and prayer.

options.text: Withdrawing from the temple and the wider public.
options.note: The opposite is true: they met daily in the temple courts and enjoyed the favor of the people.

options.text: Choosing leaders and building their own place of worship.
options.note: Luke describes teaching, fellowship, bread, and prayer, not building projects or elections.

quiz.q: What does Pentecost show about the exalted Christ?

options.text: Enthroned at God's right hand, He received and poured out the promised Spirit.
options.note: Peter says the Spirit's outpouring is proof that Jesus is exalted and reigning, verse 33.

options.text: He sent the Spirit to comfort the disciples in His absence.
options.note: The Spirit does come from the ascended Christ, but the point is that His reign is proved, not merely that the disciples are comforted.

options.text: He empowered the disciples to speak so people would admire them.
options.note: The Spirit's power was for witness to Christ and the gathering of the nations, not for the disciples' admiration.

options.text: He had not yet been given any authority from the Father.
options.note: The opposite is true: He is exalted to the right hand of God and reigns as Lord and Christ.

questions: The Spirit was poured out so the nations could hear the wonders of God in their own tongues. How does it move you that God reaches across every barrier of language and culture to make Himself known?
Peter preached Jesus crucified, risen, and exalted, and the crowd was cut to the heart. When has the good news of Jesus pierced your own heart and moved you to respond?
Peter called the crowd to repent and turn to Christ. Is there an area of your life where the Spirit is calling you to turn, and what would repentance look like there?
The first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread, and prayer. Which of these four is strongest in your own life, and which most needs to grow?
The early church shared generously with anyone in need. How might the Spirit be prompting you to hold your possessions more loosely for the sake of others?
The Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved. Who in your life might God be drawing to Himself, and how could you be part of that work this week?

translationNotes.note: Pentecost, from the Greek for fiftieth, is the Feast of Weeks or Shavuot, celebrated fifty days after Passover; a footnote links it to the Feast of Harvest in Exodus 23:16 and Exodus 34:22.
Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32, following the wording of the Greek Old Testament, applying the promised outpouring of the Spirit to the day of Pentecost.
